title: Attention Web Design: Evaluating Aesthetics Online
why: Showed users judge website aesthetics in 50 milliseconds, with verdicts correlating to ratings after extended viewing.
finding: Users rated visual appeal accurately in 50ms exposures; halo effect means attractive design predicts overlooking minor faults.

title: Aesthetics and Apparent Usability: How Do Users Initially Perceive a User Interface?
why: Tested 26 ATM UI variations with 252 participants; found aesthetics correlated more with perceived (not actual) usability.
finding: Perceived usability correlated stronger with aesthetic appeal (r=0.83) than actual usability did (r=0.47); users overlook usability issues in beautiful designs.

title: Stanford Guidelines for Web Credibility
why: Large study of web credibility assessment; 46.1% of participants rated design/look as primary credibility signal.
finding: 46.1% of participants primarily assessed site credibility by overall design appearance; visual design is the dominant trust signal.

title: The Magical Number Seven, Plus or Minus Two: Some Limits on Our Capacity for Processing Information
why: Foundational work on short-term memory capacity; proposed 7±2 chunks as span limit, though mainly a rhetorical device.
finding: Memory span limited to 7±2 items in absolute judgment tasks; memory capacity defined by chunks, not bits.

title: The Magical Number 4 in Short-Term Memory: A Reconsideration of Mental Storage Capacity
why: Meta-analysis and review arguing working memory capacity is ~4 chunks for young adults, correcting Miller's 7±2 estimate.
finding: Normal young adults retain 3-4 items in working memory when unable to form larger chunks; capacity ~4 (±1) not 7±2.

title: When Choice is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing?
why: Jam display experiment: 24-flavor booth attracted 60% but only 3% purchased; 6-flavor booth attracted 40% but 30% purchased.
finding: More options attracted more browsers (60% vs 40%) but reduced purchase rate (3% vs 30%); excess choice demotivates decisions.

title: Prospect Theory: An Analysis of Decision under Risk
why: Foundational work on loss aversion and framing effects; people need 1.5-2.5x gain to accept fair-coin gamble.
finding: Loss aversion coefficient ~2.25: losses psychologically weigh 1.5-2.5x more than equivalent gains; framing as loss makes people risk-seeking.

title: Defaults and Donation Decisions
why: Cross-European study: opt-out defaults yielded ~99% organ donation consent vs ~5% for opt-in; 60-point gap.
finding: Organ donation consent: opt-out default 99% vs opt-in 5% across European countries; defaults had ~60-point effect with no overlap in distributions.

title: Cognitive Load Theory, Learning Difficulty, and Instructional Design
why: Foundational theory: working memory processes intrinsic (task) and extraneous (design) cognitive load; limited capacity ~7 items.
finding: Working memory capacity ~7 items; intrinsic load (material difficulty) + extraneous load (design) cannot exceed capacity without learning failure.

title: Nudge: Improving Decisions About Health, Wealth, and Happiness
org: University of Chicago & Harvard Law School
why: Choice architecture framework: defaults, feedback, mapping, error handling, simplification, incentives shape decisions without restricting freedom.
finding: No neutral defaults exist; choice architecture—defaults, feedback, structure—predictably nudges decisions in intended direction while preserving choice.

title: The Fire AI Lab
why: Before and after study: aesthetics correlated with both perceived and post-use perceived usability, but actual usability did not.
finding: Pre-use perceived aesthetics correlated (r=0.70) with post-use perceived usability; actual usability had no effect on perception—halo effect confirmed.

title: Social Proof in the User Experience
why: Six principles: reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity; foundational for behavioral design.
finding: Six universal influence principles (reciprocity, commitment, social proof, authority, liking, scarcity) operate consistently across cultures and contexts.

title: Excerpt: Yes! : NPR
why: Hotel towel-reuse experiment: social-norm message (others reused) outperformed environmental message by ~25%.
finding: Social-norm message ('others reused') increased towel reuse ~25% more than environmental message; similarity effect: room-specific norm > hotel-wide norm.

title: Clinton, Obama, and the decoy effect!
why: Economist subscription example: adding decoy (print-only at $125) to [digital $59, print $125] shifted choice from 68% digital to 84% bundle.
finding: Adding inferior decoy option (print $125) redirected 84% to $125 bundle from 68% digital baseline; asymmetric dominance effect lifts revenue ~30%.

title: The 'IKEA Effect': When Labor Leads to Love
why: Four experiments (IKEA assembly, origami, Legos): effort alone increases valuation; effect disappears if task fails or is destroyed.
finding: Effort increases product valuation even for low-quality output (IKEA assembly); effect requires successful completion—failure eliminates it.

title: When More Pain Is Preferred to Less: Adding a Better End
why: Cold water immersion: 60s in 14°C vs 60s+30s in 14°C then 15°C; subjects preferred longer trial despite more total pain.
finding: Experience evaluation driven by peak pain (worst moment) and end state, not total duration; adding better ending increases repeat preference.

title: Hick's law
why: Reaction time increases logarithmically with choice count: RT = a + b·log₂(n); doubling choices doesn't double decision time.
finding: Reaction time = constant + coefficient × log₂(number of choices); logarithmic growth means menu size moderately increases decision latency.

title: Zeigarnik Effect
why: Cafe observation: waitstaff recalled open orders far better than completed ones; interrupted tasks remembered longer.
finding: Incomplete tasks held in memory ~2x better than completed ones when person has intrinsic interest; effect sensitive to trivial tasks and extrinsic rewards.

title: Gorillas in Our Midst: Sustained Inattentional Blindness for Dynamic Events
why: Basketball video: 50% of viewers failed to notice gorilla walking through the court; attention determines what we perceive.
finding: 50% failed to notice unexpected gorilla during attentional task; change blindness reveals perception limited to attended objects, not complete scenes.

title: Processing Fluency and Aesthetic Pleasure
why: Ease of cognitive processing drives aesthetic preference; symmetric, simple, clear stimuli liked more than complex ones.
finding: Processing fluency (mental ease) determines aesthetic preference; easy-to-process stimuli judged as more beautiful, truer, and preferred.

title: Ego Depletion and Self-Regulatory Failure: A Resource Model of Self-Control
why: Ego depletion: initial self-control task reduced persistence on second task; decision fatigue depletes mental resources.
finding: Self-control acts as a muscle: initial restraint reduced subsequent persistence (puzzle-solving); important caveat: 2016 replication with 2,141 participants found no effect.

title: Availability: A Heuristic for Judging Frequency and Probability
why: People judge frequency by ease of recalling examples (availability); systematic bias because memorability ≠ actual frequency.
finding: People estimate event frequency by mental ease of recall, not actual probability; creates systematic biases because visibility and frequency diverge.

title: Effects of a Favor and Liking on Compliance
why: Free Coke study: receiving unsolicited favor doubled raffle ticket purchases even among subjects who disliked the favor-giver.
finding: Unsolicited favor (free Coke) doubled raffle ticket purchases; reciprocity norm obligates return favor regardless of liking or relationship.

title: Robert Cialdini: Authority Matters if You Want to Pre-Suade Others
why: Authority-wearing experimenter: 65% of subjects administered seemingly lethal shocks, showing authority overrides moral judgment.
finding: 65% of subjects delivered maximum shocks when instructed by authority figure; authority principle overrides personal morality and conscience.

title: Serial Position Effect (Primary & recency)
why: Serial position effect: first items (primacy) and last items (recency) recalled better than middle items (forgetting curve).
finding: Recall U-shaped by list position: primacy (first items stored in long-term memory) + recency (last items in working memory); middle items forgotten most.

title: Über die Wirkung von Bereichsbildungen im Spurenfeld
why: Distinctive (isolated) items in a list remembered far better; effect due to focused attention and deeper encoding.
finding: Distinctive items recalled ~30% better; isolation captures attention, deepens encoding, and reduces interference from similar items.

title: The Goal-Gradient Hypothesis Resurrected: Purchase Acceleration, Illusionary Goal Progress, and Customer Retention
why: Coffee-stamp study: participants accelerated purchases as rewards approached; illusory progress (head-start) increased engagement.
finding: Customers accelerate purchase rate as goal approaches (goal-gradient effect); illusory progress via head-start increases retention and effort without real progress.

title: The Endowed Progress Effect: How Artificial Advancement Increases Effort
why: Pre-filled progress (2 of 10 stamps) compressed perceived distance to goal and boosted commitment dramatically.
finding: Endowed progress (head-start of 2/10 stamps) increased completion rates by compressing psychological goal distance; effect activates goal-gradient acceleration.

title: Using Eye Tracking to Understand Banner Blindness and Improve Website Design
why: Eye-tracking reveals users systematically ignore banner ads; bright, flashing, irrelevant banners suffer worst blindness.
finding: Users' eye gaze avoids banner ads systematically; irrelevant, bright, or flashing banners suffer worst blindness; text ads read ~2x more than display ads.

title: When Product Assortment Leads to Choice Overload: A Conceptual Review and Meta-Analysis
why: Meta-analysis of 99 observations (N=7,202): identified task difficulty, complexity, preference uncertainty, decision goal as choice-overload moderators.
finding: Meta-analysis (99 conditions) found choice-overload effect significant when moderators present (difficulty, complexity, uncertainty); counters Scheibehenne zero-effect finding.

title: The Psychology of Waiting Lines
why: Foundational work: occupied time feels shorter; waits perceived differently by engagement, knowledge, fairness; applies to loading states, processing feedback.
finding: Occupied time (active engagement) feels shorter than unoccupied time equally long; engaged waits feel 2x-3x shorter than empty waits.

title: The Labor Illusion: How Operational Transparency Increases Perceived Value
why: Flight-search study: users with visible progress accepted longer waits (preferred wait over instant result); perceived effort increases valuation.
finding: Visible operational work (progress display) increased perceived value; users willing to wait longer when they see site 'working hard' on their behalf.

title: Faster Progress Bars: Manipulating Perceived Duration with Visual Illusions
why: Animated progress bars with visual illusions (ripple direction, acceleration phases) perceived as ~10% faster without changing actual speed.
finding: Leftward ripples and progressive acceleration in progress bars reduce perceived wait time by ~10%; humans perceive nonlinear time passage.

title: Extraneous Factors in Judicial Decisions
why: Analysis of 1,100+ parole decisions: early-day/post-break grants ~65%, late-day grants ~0%; tired judges rule in favor of status quo.
finding: Parole grant rate 65% morning vs ~0% late-day; decision fatigue after repeated choices increases status quo bias; judges need cognitive rest.

title: Patients' Memories of Painful Medical Treatments: Real-time and Retrospective Evaluations of Colonoscopy Discomfort
why: Colonoscopy study: adding 3 minutes of low discomfort at end reduced reported experience discomfort vs shorter procedure; peak+end dominates memory.
finding: Extended procedure rated less unpleasant than shorter one; memory of experience driven by peak pain + end state, not total duration or average.

title: The Information Capacity of the Human Motor System in Controlling the Amplitude of Movement
why: Movement time = a + b·log₂(distance/width); foundational for touch targets, button sizing, mouse control; logarithmic not linear relationship.
finding: Reaction time MT = constant + coefficient × log₂(D/W); larger targets reduce selection time logarithmically; 2x distance ≠ 2x time.

title: The Design of Everyday Things
why: Introduced affordances concept: properties of objects that determine how they're used; feedback, mapping, constraints reduce cognitive load.
finding: Affordances (perceived/actual properties) guide usage; good design uses feedback, mapping, constraints, and conceptual models to align user mental models.

title: Festinger's Law
why: Inconsistent beliefs produce psychological discomfort; people rationalize to reduce dissonance rather than changing behavior (especially after sacrifice).
finding: Cognitive dissonance (conflicting beliefs) triggers rationalization not behavior change; effect strongest when past sacrifice was largest (not smallest).

title: Treatise on Physiological Optics
why: Visual perception is inference from fragmentary sensory data + stored knowledge; illusions reveal perception goes beyond data; perception ≠ sensation.
finding: Visual perception = unconscious inference from sensory data + knowledge; illusions reveal perception involves unconscious logical reasoning, not just sensation.

title: Distributed Practices in Verbal Recall Tasks: A Review and Quantitative Synthesis
why: Meta-analysis: spaced practice superior to massed; optimal gap ~20-40% for 1-week test, 5-10% for 1-year test; too-short gaps worse than too-long.
finding: Optimal review interval = 10-20% of retention period; too-short intervals more harmful than too-long; spaced review ~50% more effective than massed.

title: Stroop Effect
why: Naming color is slower when word (different color) interferes; reading automatic, color-naming requires effort; interference reveals attention conflicts.
finding: Conflicting word-color (red word in green ink) slows color-naming by ~30-40%; automatic reading interferes with controlled attention task.

title: Status Quo Bias in Decision Making
why: Framing option as status quo increases choice rate vs neutral framing; pervasive bias in insurance, retirement, and health decisions.
finding: Framing as status quo increases selection disproportionately; employees stick with default health insurance regardless of plan quality.

title: Commitment and Consistency
why: Small initial request (petition) led to 76% compliance with large later request vs 17% without foot-in-door; commitment shifts self-perception.
finding: Small commitment (signing petition) increased large request compliance from 17% to 76%; consistency principle: prior commitment signals identity.

title: Predicting Users' First Impressions of Website Aesthetics with a Quantification of Perceived Visual Complexity and Colorfulness
why: 450 websites rated; visual complexity + colorfulness explain ~50% of aesthetic appeal variance at 500ms exposure; preferences vary by demographic.
finding: Visual complexity + colorfulness predict 50% of aesthetic appeal variance in first 500ms; female users prefer more colorful sites than male users.
